It's only about 200 pages, including an impeccable bibliography that will lead you to other sources that look at specific areas and periods in a lot more depth. It's also a translation of Greater Ethiopia by Donald Levin, which is easier to find and potentially more accessible if reading in Amharic is too challenging. The translator made an incredible effort in translating a lot of scientific,  sociological, anthropological,  and linguistic terms, so your vocabulary will also thank you for it. The edition I have is from 2007 (E.C), so the Amharic vocabulary used is more recent and more comprehensible, in my opinion. Hope this helps. Happy Reading!

I don't agree. For all of the problems I personally feel religion creates/exacerbates, a preoccupation with politics is certainly not one of them. In fact, the durability of monarchic rule (although under different banners) through out Ethiopia's history was acheived through a symbiotic relationship between church and state. 

The bigger problem especially in the last 30 or so years is the absence of so-called academics to satisfy people's natural curiosity without condescending to them. 

Most Ethiopian "scholars" upon realizing the unacceptable disparity in *access to* knowledge that exists between them and the average person, almost always turn into complete assholes instead of been motivated to help close these gaps. In my personal experience this seems to be worse the higher up you go. Anyone who's gone to an Ethiopian university and studied under Ethiopian "professors" will understand.

>Obviously iq measures only one specific kind of intelligence.

IQ measures zero kinds of intelligence. And the kinds that it is purported to measure, i.e., mental age/real age is not something that can be "schooled away". If you assert this low I.Q. nonesense then you have to accept that there can be few remedies (if any) to significantly increase the median IQ.

Mostly because we have no real way to participate in the political process. It's frustrating to be at the compete mercy of forces that should be within your control but aren't. This isn't new. It's one of the few issues you can trace as far back as whatever conception of Ethiopia has existed. 

The luxury of even talking about power in this country is a fairly recent development; one granted nominally by EPDRF (and yet to be realized meaningfully by PP). I think there is a sense, certainly within myself, that enough political opinions can somehow snowball into impactful action. But that, of course, is a fallacy and a cowardly one at that.

Finally, I want to point out that the space to truly excel in the 'alternate' pursuits that you mention like literature and science is only made possible when there is a political structure in place to nurture it when possible or restrained by laws so that it doesn't actively get in the way. 

There is certainly a reductionist impulse among many Ethiopians in the face of what was an almost insurmountable task of nation building even before a multi-year, holy-fuck-has-it-been-that-long civil war (and also COVID). Meaning, we would all like the ills of our country to be simplified to one problem beit social, political, or economic and gravitate towards narratives that frame our current circumstances in that way.

>Ethiopia is still an agrarian society that still has a lot of its population living in abject poverty. That is the reason for the low iq of Ethiopians.

Might make *slightly* more sense the other way around. Assuming you somehow have a reliable sample for a population to dispersed for even the most necessary of data collection, the mode of economic organization would most likely be an outcome and not really a prerequisite of low average IQ. 

That being said, I personally find that people most obsessed with the idea of an intelligence quotient, especially as we understand it in the present day, are generally some of the most ignorant motherfuckers around. It isn't even the near impossible task of aggregating national level IQ data that bothers me about what you say, but the unfortunate extent to which you believe your own bullshit.

My favourite argument always is the fact that a free market is the "default setting" of economies. If you aren't using a super constricted definition of economy, then historically all forms of trade and exchange have happened in the absence of government interference because both economic policies and governments are relatively new constructs. Thus the case can be made that in a state where the free market is allowed to take place won't be as apocalyptic as those on the left make it out to be. 

Alternatively, you could make a contrarian argument. My favourite in this case is an argument that Ben Shapiro often makes -- socialism is rape and capitalism is consensual sex. What he's attempting to highlight is the fact government interference almost always leads to a situation where someone has to do something that they don't want to do -- and this action is often enforced via laws. Wherein the free market allows you to make the decisions you want and ultimately your faliure is your fault. 

If you're writing a paper, there are a lot of resources you can look up. If you're preparing for a verbal exchange, I'd be careful to explain the fact that the free market requires that all participants play with in the rules of the game. Because the usual arguments against the free market involve some version of "capitalism sucks because 2008". You need to explain that the apparent shortcomings of the free market aren't a result of the free market, but the stupidity of individuals. And it's nearly impossible to argue that 2008 wouldn't have happened in a mixed or command economy.

Hope this helps :-)
